item.title: Before the Earth moves. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The earthquake tragedy in Colombia last month should make Bangladesh ask a question that has little to do with predicting earthquakes: What happens when most of a nation's population, opportunity, and institutional capacity become concentrated in one city?
The United Nations projects Dhaka to become the world's largest city by 2050, with a population exceeding 50 million. Bangladesh already struggles with congestion, housing shortages, groundwater stress, pollution, inadequate sanitation, and enormous pressure on public services. Add tens of millions of people to this urban system, and earthquake vulnerability becomes only one dimension of a much larger human-development challenge.
Bangladesh already has projects designed to strengthen secondary cities, transportation corridors, and areas outside Dhaka. But the scale of the coming transformation requires something larger.
We should stop thinking primarily about moving people and start moving opportunities.
Start with those whose jobs may not survive
Walk through Dhaka and one sees an extraordinary amount of human effort.
A rickshaw puller pedals through extreme heat. A day labourer waits each morning hoping someone needs him. A young graduate rides a bicycle for deliveries because he cannot find work matching his education. A garment worker wonders whether automation will eventually replace part of her job. A rural worker leaves home because Dhaka appears to offer the only realistic path toward higher income.
These people are often described statistically as “labour.”
They are something much more important: Bangladesh's human capital.
The question is whether Bangladesh will continue using millions of people in occupations producing relatively little economic value and offering limited upward mobility or invest in enabling those same people to build the next economy.
Consider the rickshaw puller. The policy objective should not be to ban his rickshaw. That simply destroys income.
Ask instead: What could this person be doing 10 years from now?
Could he become a construction technician? A plumber? A logistics worker? A solar installer? A water-treatment operator? An emergency-response worker?
Then ask the more important question: What would it take to get him there?
That is human development.
Bangladesh may need housing and infrastructure for tens of millions of additional urban residents over the coming decades.
That sounds like a burden. It could also represent one of the largest employment opportunities in the country's history.
Building a network of 20 or 30 major economic centres would require enormous numbers of electricians, plumbers, welders, machine operators, construction workers, engineers, drivers, healthcare workers, water technicians, teachers, maintenance workers, and logistics professionals, among countless others.
Bangladesh already has much of the labour. The challenge is transforming skills.
Imagine a national program under which workers in vulnerable or low-productivity occupations receive paid training for three to 12 months. Training would be tied directly to employment.
The worker would not receive a certificate and then be told to search for a job. Infrastructure contracts receiving public support would commit to hiring qualified graduates.
The pathway becomes: Informal work → training → skilled employment → stable income → housing → financial inclusion → family security.
Urbanization then becomes a mechanism for social mobility.
Don't build another Dhaka
The objective should not be to create another megacity containing 30 million people.
Bangladesh needs a network.
Imagine economic centres distributed along existing and future rail, highway, and river corridors.
Some could specialize in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. Others in advanced textiles, food processing, logistics, electronics, renewable energy, technology, or light manufacturing.
Each would combine employment with housing, hospitals, schools, universities, parks, public transportation, and digital infrastructure.
That distinction is essential.
People do not move because planners draw circles on maps. They move because they can build better lives.
A family will leave Dhaka voluntarily when another city offers a good job, affordable home, safe school, reliable hospital, clean water, and reasonable transportation.
Bangladesh should therefore not attempt to redistribute population. It should redistribute reasons for people to choose where they live.
Water must come before homes
Water security should determine where these new centres grow.
Dhaka illustrates what happens when population growth outruns environmental infrastructure. The World Bank's current Metro Dhaka Water Security and Resilience Program describes serious pollution of rivers and canals resulting from rapid urbanization, inadequate sanitation, industrial discharge, and waste.
Bangladesh cannot sustainably replicate this pattern across the country. The next generation of cities should reverse the sequence.
Before approving hundreds of thousands of apartments, establish where their water will come from. Protect wetlands. Build reservoirs. Capture rainwater. Treat sewage. Recycle wastewater for industry. Protect groundwater recharge. Separate stormwater from sewage. Monitor industrial discharge digitally.
Bangladesh is one of the most water-rich landscapes on Earth, yet millions of citizens still experience problems involving safe drinking water.
That paradox demonstrates that water security is not merely about how much water a country possesses. It is about whether infrastructure delivers clean water to people when and where they need it.
Urban policy is health policy
The benefits would extend directly into national health.
A hospital treats disease after it occurs. A well-designed city can prevent some disease before the patient reaches the hospital.
Clean water reduces waterborne illness. Modern sanitation reduces exposure to pathogens. Cleaner transportation improves air quality. Better drainage reduces stagnant contaminated water. Trees and shaded streets reduce dangerous heat exposure. Walkable communities encourage physical activity. Shorter commutes give parents more time to their children. Formal employment makes health insurance and retirement savings more achievable. Distributed medical centres reduce the need for families across Bangladesh to travel to Dhaka for treatment.
For a country with limited healthcare resources, prevention through better living conditions may be among the highest-return health investments available.
Then there is the earthquake.
The magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia last month demonstrated again how quickly buildings, roads, and ordinary lives can be transformed by seismic disaster.
Bangladesh cannot know exactly when a major earthquake will strike the region. But Dhaka's vulnerability is well documented.
The answer cannot simply be more ambulances and rescue equipment.
If tens of millions of people, major hospitals, government institutions, financial organizations, and businesses remain concentrated within the same metropolitan region, Bangladesh is effectively concentrating national risk.
Developing multiple economic centres is therefore similar to diversifying an investment portfolio. If one region suffers catastrophe, the country continues functioning. Decentralization becomes national insurance.
Give Dhaka room to breathe
This strategy does not require abandoning Dhaka. It may be the best way to save it.
As future population growth increasingly occurs elsewhere, Dhaka can begin repairing the damage created by decades of uncontrolled expansion.
Unsafe buildings can gradually be replaced. Canals can be restored. Wetlands can be protected. Emergency roads can be widened. Schools and hospitals can be retrofitted. Waterways can again become environmental assets rather than drains.
Dhaka could become safer without becoming economically irrelevant.
The objective is not to weaken Dhaka. It is to make Bangladesh stronger than Dhaka alone.
Dr Mazher Mir is a Bangladeshi writer with over three decades of work on socio-economic and human development issues.

item.title: Going beyond relief for the Rohingya. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For about a decade, Bangladesh has carried an enormous humanitarian responsibility by sheltering hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees who fled persecution in Myanmar -- a feat that has proven to be both commendable and challenging.
While the ultimate solution remains their safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation, the reality is that their displacement has continued for far too long. In such circumstances, ensuring that the Rohingya have opportunities to build skills and prepare for a better future is both practical and humane.
The newly launched skills development program for 1,000 Rohingya in Cox’s Bazar is, therefore, a welcome initiative.
With training in areas including tailoring, dressmaking, block printing, batik, mobile phone servicing, gas burner repair, and climate-smart agriculture, alongside essential soft skills, the program can help participants become more self-reliant and better prepared for future livelihood opportunities.
This is especially important because humanitarian assistance, while essential, cannot be the only focus when a crisis becomes prolonged. Aid can keep people alive and meet immediate needs, but skills, education, and livelihood opportunities can provide people with dignity, confidence, and the capacity to rebuild their lives.
For Bangladesh -- which continues to shoulder significant social, economic, and environmental pressures from hosting the Rohingya -- programs such as this also demonstrate that supporting the refugees does not have to mean simply providing relief.
We can, within the limitations of the camp environment and existing regulations, help prepare a generation for a future beyond dependency.
At the same time, such initiatives must complement and not replace the international community’s responsibility to resolve the crisis.
Bangladesh cannot be expected to host the Rohingya indefinitely. Greater international pressure must be maintained on Myanmar to create conditions for safe and dignified repatriation.
Until that becomes possible, however, it is a wise idea to do some good for the community’s future. Skills development is an investment in people, and the Rohingya surely deserve that.

item.title: Getting unfit buses off our roads. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That authorities are now saying unfit, or “rickety,” buses will not be allowed to operate, even when they possess fitness certificates, is certainly a welcome development, on paper.
For years, Dhaka’s commuters have been forced to share the roads with buses that are simply not fit to be called roadworthy -- with common defects like rusting bodies, broken windows, worn-out tires, faulty doors, and poorly maintained engines.
But while the acknowledgement of the problem is encouraging, this is a promise we have heard before.
The real problem is not a lack of rules: Bangladesh already has laws and regulatory mechanisms requiring vehicles to meet minimum safety standards; the glaring failure has always been enforcement.
A bus that is visibly unsafe should never have been on the roads in the first place. Additionally, if a vehicle deteriorates after receiving certification, there must be mechanisms to identify it and take it off the road.
This is why the latest initiative must go beyond occasional drives and headline-making announcements.
Fitness certificates must reflect the actual condition of vehicles rather than becoming a formality. Officials responsible for approving unsafe buses must also face accountability.
At the same time, bus owners need practical facilities and sufficient time to carry out repairs -- particularly as authorities move maintenance activities towards the planned Purbachal depot.
The reported plan to develop the facility is encouraging, but infrastructure must translate into better maintenance standards, not merely relocation.
Most importantly, enforcement cannot stop after the initial crackdown. Owners must know that an unsafe bus will be taken off the road -- regardless of its paperwork, influence, or age.
Dhaka’s commuters have waited long enough. We have heard these promises before. Now it is time to get it done and, more importantly, to ensure that the rules are strictly and consistently followed.

item.title: Are we asking the right questions about climate migration?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Climate migration is no longer a distant phenomenon or a future concern; it is already reshaping communities, economies, and urban areas across the world.
Due to its unique geographic location, Bangladesh remains particularly vulnerable to adverse climate hazards. Every year, people affected by both slow and sudden events - including uneven precipitation, droughts, flash floods, cyclones, salinity intrusion, river erosion, and other environmental pressures -- leave their homes in search of livelihood opportunities elsewhere.
As these events continue to intensify, climate migration is increasingly becoming a development challenge. However, while considerable attention is being given to identifying climate migrants and estimating their numbers, far less attention is being paid to a more pressing question: How should Bangladesh prepare its towns and cities to manage increasing climate-linked mobility?
The lack of an agreed definition remains one of the most debated issues in climate migration discourse. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) defines climate migration as the movement of people who are compelled, or choose, to leave their habitual place of residence because of sudden or gradual environmental changes associated with climate change.
International frameworks have taken different approaches to understanding climate-related mobility. For example, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) refers to climate change-induced displacement, migration, and planned relocation rather than relying on a specific definition of “climate migrant.”
This reflects the complexity of migration decisions, which are often shaped by multiple and overlapping environmental, economic, social, and political factors, making it difficult to attribute mobility solely to climate change.
Despite the ongoing debate over definitions, the scale of climate-linked mobility continues to grow.
According to the World Bank’s latest Groundswell report, more than 216 million people could move within their own countries by 2050 due to climate change. Bangladesh alone could experience as many as 19.9 million internal climate migrants by mid-century.
A joint assessment conducted by the Bangladesh government and IOM in 2025 estimates that nearly five million people are currently living in situations of internal displacement linked to natural disasters.
Whatever the exact number of climate-linked displaced persons today or in the coming decades, people are already moving, and Bangladesh must prepare for the consequences.
Most climate-affected households, particularly displaced populations, relocate within the country, often to nearby secondary towns and urban centres. A significant number eventually move to major cities.
According to the Migration Policy Institute, approximately 400,000 people arrive in Dhaka every year. However, migration decisions are rarely driven by a single factor.
Climate and environmental pressures often interact with economic opportunities, social networks, access to services, and other considerations in shaping mobility decisions.
Migration does not necessarily end vulnerability. Many migrants or displaced households settle in informal settlements where housing conditions are poor and access to services remains limited.
Men who once relied on agriculture, fishing, or other rural occupations usually become day labourers because their existing skills do not match the demands of urban labour markets.
Women often enter low-paid domestic work or other informal sectors. Economic hardship pushes many children into labour, compromising their education and limiting their future opportunities.
The consequences of climate-linked displacement and migration are beyond livelihoods and often impacts kinship, neighbourhood feelings, weakens community support systems, and creates psychological stress.
Drawing on Arjun Appadurai’s concept “capacity to aspire,” climate displacement affects not only the people’s circumstances but limits their capacity to imagine a better future.
When households become trapped in daily wages for survival, their ability to pursue long-term aspirations is diminished. Yet mental health and psychosocial wellbeing remain largely overlooked in climate migration discussions.
At the same time, receiving cities and towns face increasing pressures in managing water supply, sanitation, healthcare, education, housing, transportation, waste management, and other essential services for growing populations, often with limited financial and institutional capacities.
Climate migration therefore is not only a humanitarian issue; it is equally an urban governance and development challenge.
Recognising these realities, the government of Bangladesh adopted the National Strategy on Internal Displacement Management in 2021. Development partners, international organizations, NGOs, and research institutions have also invested considerable effort in responding to climate-linked migration.
However, one aspect of the current discussion deserves closer attention.
Increasingly, municipal authorities, development partners, and researchers seek to identify climate migrants and estimate their numbers in specific towns and cities.
While understanding population movements is important for planning services, infrastructure, and future urban growth, it is important to distinguish between estimating population movements and categorizing individuals as climate migrants.
Estimating population movements supports planning; labelling individuals as climate migrants raises practical and policy concerns.
Migration and displacement are often shaped by a combination of environmental, economic, social, demographic, and personal considerations. A family displaced by river erosion, for example, may also move in search of livelihood opportunities or to join relatives already living in urban areas.
Likewise, even when displacement follows a cyclone, such movement may also reflect governance failure, including weak embankment management, poor water management, and inadequate investment in local adaptation.
This complexity makes identifying an individual as a climate migrant or climate-displaced person far from straightforward.
The question is not whether climate change contributes to displacement and migration, but whether mobility can be attributed to climate factors alone.
This is particularly important because the global debate on climate migration extends beyond human mobility to encompass issues of shared responsibility, national adaptation efforts, development financing, and differing positions among industrialised, developing and least developed countries regarding greenhouse gas emissions.
Furthermore, even if the UNFCCC were to adopt a universally accepted definition of climate migration tomorrow, practical challenges would remain unresolved at the domestic level.
How would authorities distinguish climate migration from movement driven by economic necessity, social networks, family-related factors, or governance failures?
More importantly, it is worth asking what practical benefit such categorization would bring. While identifying climate migrants may be necessary in certain circumstances to facilitate targeted support and protection, categorization alone does not improve livelihoods or guarantee access to services.
Even if climate migrants could be identified with complete accuracy, the more fundamental challenge would remain unchanged: Whether local economies, urban systems, and public institutions are capable of accommodating increasing population movements in an inclusive and sustainable manner.
The challenge is not merely identifying people on the move, but ensuring that towns and cities are prepared to absorb them through adequate jobs, housing, infrastructure, and public services.
Without such capacities, a label by itself offers little practical value.
This is not an argument against data. Reliable estimates of population movement remain essential for planning and policymaking.
The argument is simply that counting people and labelling people are not the same thing. For planning purposes, we need to estimate people. For governance purposes, we need to serve people.
The more relevant policy question is not whether an individual can be conclusively identified as a climate migrant. Rather, it is whether local institutions, urban systems, and public services are capable of responding to increasing population movements in an inclusive and sustainable manner.
The discussion therefore needs to move beyond identifying climate migrants and towards strengthening the capacity of towns and cities to manage increasing population movements.
Climate-related mobility is inherently a multi-sectoral issue. Housing, healthcare, livelihoods, water supply, sanitation, waste management, and education cannot be addressed in isolation.
Rather, they require coordinated planning, investment, and institutional readiness to ensure that growing populations can be accommodated in a sustainable manner.
Strengthening local economies and creating opportunities beyond a few major cities can also help secondary cities absorb additional populations more effectively.
Urban planning should therefore anticipate future population movements and consider the additional demand for services, infrastructure, housing, and employment that may emerge over time.
Such investments will not only support people who move but also benefit existing residents and the wider urban ecosystem.
In the longer term, strengthening the capacity of secondary towns may contribute to a more balanced economic opportunities, public services, and investments across the country.
As climate impacts intensify in the coming decades, human mobility will become an increasingly important feature of Bangladesh’s development landscape.
The debate over definitions and classifications will undoubtedly continue. The important question therefore is whether Bangladesh is adequately preparing its towns and cities to manage increasing climate migrants in a way that supports both people and places.
Md Abul Basar is an Anthropologist and Governance Expert, serving as Team Leader at Swisscontact Bangladesh, a Switzerland-based international organization. He can be reached at abul.basar@swisscontact.org.

item.title: Can we expect a better labour market?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Malaysia’s labour market is set to reopen after a prolonged suspension marked by scrutiny, political transitions, and deep uncertainty.
For years, the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has been surrounded by allegations of syndication, excessive recruitment costs, limited access to recruitment services, and practices that left workers bearing the greatest burden of a system over which they had little control.
During the tenure of Sheikh Hasina's government, the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia became increasingly entangled with political and business interests. The recruitment arrangements developed during this period are often linked to the emergence of a syndication model that would later concentrate access to the Malaysian labour market among a select group of agencies. What began under one set of political actors, however, did not end with them.
Over the years, other parliamentarians and politically-connected interests became part of the wider ecosystem, allowing the model to persist and evolve. The problem, therefore, cannot simply be reduced to one minister, one political party, or one period of government.
At its core was a recruitment structure in which access became concentrated, while aspiring migrant workers bore the consequences through high costs, uncertainty, and limited choice.
For Bangladeshi workers, these were never simply matters of policy or politics. They meant years of waiting, borrowing money, paying recruitment fees, and placing their hopes in a system that often seemed designed around everything except the worker.
The consequences became painfully visible on May 31, 2024, when hundreds of aspiring migrant workers gathered at Dhaka airport, waiting to leave for Malaysia. Their recruiting agencies had failed to provide their air tickets before the deadline set by the Malaysian government expired that day. Malaysia closed its labour market to Bangladeshi workers from June 1. It was yet another painful repetition of a cycle in which migrant workers were left to bear the consequences of decisions over which they had little control.
However, the long suspension also created something that had been missing for years: An opportunity to rethink the system.
As Bangladesh emerged from 15 years under the same ruling party and moved through a political transition towards a new governing arrangement, there was hope that reopening the Malaysian labour market could mean more than simply restarting recruitment. Perhaps this time, recruitment could be more transparent. Perhaps agencies would be selected according to clear and measurable standards rather than political or business connections. Perhaps workers would no longer have to pay disproportionate sums simply for the opportunity to work.
There was, in other words, room for change.
But now, as Malaysia prepares to reopen the market with a fresh list of 25 recruiting agencies, an uncomfortable question remains: Does changing the names on the list amount to changing the system?
If the selection process continues to rely on a limited pool of agencies without sufficiently examining their recruitment history, worker complaints, fee structures, treatment of migrants, and compliance with fair recruitment standards, then the underlying problem remains. The same concentration of power could simply return under a different configuration.
And if that happens, it will be the migrant worker who pays the price once again.
The lesson from the previous system should not simply be that too few agencies were involved. It should be that concentrating recruitment among a select group without strong safeguards and accountability creates the conditions for exploitation. The number of agencies matters, but so does how they are selected, monitored, and held accountable.
A credible reopening should therefore begin with transparent selection criteria. Agencies should be assessed not only on their licences or administrative capacity, but also on their track record in fair recruitment practices, worker protection, compliance with agreed recruitment costs, and grievance handling.
Workers should be able to understand what they are paying for, where their money is going, what employment has been promised to them, and where they can seek help when those promises are not honoured.
This also requires stronger accountability on both sides of the migration corridor. Bangladesh and Malaysia need mechanisms to monitor recruitment practices, address worker complaints, and ensure that agencies or employers who violate agreed standards face meaningful consequences. Fair recruitment cannot depend on goodwill alone; it requires systems capable of enforcing it.
Most importantly, recruitment should no longer be treated as a transaction in which the worker is simply the final commodity being moved between two labour markets. A worker is not merely a unit of labour to be recruited, transported, and placed. The recruitment process determines the debt they carry, the expectations they leave home with and, ultimately, the vulnerability they may face at their destination.
A reopened labour market will inevitably be welcomed as an opportunity for thousands of Bangladeshis seeking employment abroad. It should be. Malaysia has long been an important destination for Bangladeshi workers, and legitimate employment opportunities can transform the lives of families.
But reopening the labour market cannot become the destination in itself.
The real test will come after the first worker leaves Bangladesh: How much did they pay? How accurately did the job match the promise? What protection did they receive? And who will stand beside them if something goes wrong?
If the answers remain unchanged, then we have not reopened a labour market; we have simply reopened an old system.
For years, Bangladeshi migrant workers have carried the cost of recruitment failures through debt, deception, uncertainty, and lost opportunities. They deserve more than a new list of recruiting agencies. They deserve a recruitment system in which transparency is the rule, accountability is enforceable, and dignity is treated as a condition of migration, not an afterthought.
Efrita Jahan is currently part of the BRAC Migration Program.

Muneeba hails 'belief' after shaky Pakistan trounce Thailand in Women's Asia Cup. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DUBAI: Pakistan opener Muneeba Ali hailed the team’s “belief” after the side endured a chaotic batting show to trounce Thailand in their Women’s Asia Cup opener at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Tuesday night.

Pakistan’s batting woes exposed themselves once again as they were reduced to 23-3 within the powerplay after captain Fatima Sana won the toss. However, wicket-keeper-batter Muneeba stabilised the innings, and dug in to produce a sturdy knock of 54 runs off 52 balls that gave Pakistan a 35-run win.

Muneeba provided some much-needed relief to the batting line-up, braving the hot and humid conditions in Dubai.

“When wickets kept falling in the powerplay, we knew if we got a good partnership and kept on scoring runs, it would put the bowlers under pressure, and give us opportunities to score,” she said in the post-match press conference.

“That’s what my strategy was.” the bespectacled southpaw added, when asked about how she navigated the innings.

“In the past, if wickets fell in the powerplay, we wouldn’t be able to come back into the match.

“Today the difference was that even when we lost wickets, the team kept belief and tried setting a total which would be defendable against the opposition on this pitch.”

Pakistan’s propensity for batting collapses cost them greatly in the Women’s T20 World Cup in June, where they managed only one win in their group, against the Netherlands.

A lack of momentum and frequent collapses led them to humbling 64 and 113-run losses against India and Australia respectively, while a mid-innings stutter against Bangladesh left the team at 100-8, unable to chase an achievable 124.

The bilateral series that followed against Sri Lanka proved to be better from a batting perspective, especially with a new opening pair in Muneeba and Shawal Zulfiqar. However, the line-up still came up short, as Sri Lanka chased both targets of 170-odd in the first two matches to take the series.

“Obviously, in the last few T20 series we played before the Sri Lanka, our batting unit did not click as such and we had our struggles,” said Muneeba.

“We have been working on those issues in camps, to make sure we don’t repeat the same mistakes, and bring in some different options in our batting.”

Pakistan had found themselves in trouble early on, faltering at 6-2 at the two-over mark after a double wicket maiden by Thipatcha Phuttawong.

After a stodgy powerplay, Muneeba and Sadaf Shamas set about a rebuild, stitching a 54-run partnership to ease the early-innings jitters. Shamas, trying to cut a wider delivery, fell for a run-a-ball 2o. Fatima, who has been reliable with the bat in recent times, fell for a duck in the same over to put Pakistan in a real spot of bother.

Muneeba reached her half-century in the 15th over. Though a flurry of late wickets blotted the flow of runs, Muneeba’s knock and a useful cameo of 12 not out off four balls by Tuba Hassan took Pakistan to a first-innings score of 119-9.

Muneeba said after the match that though the team had aimed to put up a score of at least 140 on the board, they knew that 120 or 130-plus would be defendable by the team’s bowling line-up.

Spin trap

And defend they did; skipper Fatima was validated for her choice of batting first as Pakistan reduced Thailand to 84-8 for their 20 overs, owing to an expert spin-strangle.

Sadia Iqbal took a double wicket maiden of her own as Thailand found themselves at 6-2 at the two-over mark, mirroring Pakistan’s position at the corresponding point in their own innings.

The next 11 overs then amounted to only 37 runs as Pakistan’s spin attack tightened their grip on the match with disciplined bowling, giving nothing away to the batters.

Chasing 120,Thailand were 42-4 at the 13th over mark, requiring almost 12 runs an over thereon.

Nashra Sandhu’s introduction after the powerplay proved key with the veteran conceding only six runs across her four overs, she picked up the wicket of Natthakan Chantham with an excellent flighted delivery that turned to miss the bat and smash the off-stump.

“I didn’t have any complicated plans,” said Nashra in a post-match reflection video posted on Pakistan Cricket Board’s social media handles, featuring her and team-mate Tuba Hassan.

“I knew there was bounce and turn in the pitch, and that it was keeping low. I just had to bowl at the right spots, the pitch did the rest.”

Tuba had a decisive all-round impact on the match, featuring her emphatic stint with the bat and two wickets for 17 runs in her four overs. In the field, she nailed a direct-hit with razor-sharp accuracy to run Naomi Hamilton out.

“My plan was simple; bowl wicket-to-wicket and vary the pace as much as possible, because we also need to prepare for the next match,” said Tuba.

She added that the conditions were very humid, making them a little “tricky”, as the ball would slip easily.

“These are exactly the things we need to learn from, so that we can make less mistakes in the next matches and play better.”

For Thailand, the defeat marked the end of their Asia Cup campaign, having already played their first two group-stage matches that ended in a win against Hong Kong and a drubbing at the hands of India.

With first points on the board, Pakistan now turn their attention to the ever-crucial fixture against arch-rivals India on Saturday.

item.description:
A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations.

View the full agenda here.

4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition

Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition.

“The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said.

She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage.

“During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition.

“250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said.

4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins

4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food

Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”.

“Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said.

Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem.

3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive

Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”.

He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential.

He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps… that will allow […] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.”

3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official

Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce.

He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition.

He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc.

3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative

Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition.

“We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled.

“It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added.

“Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added.

3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins

A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun.

3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official

Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue.

“Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting.

“ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.”

3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’

The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”.

Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition.

“Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said.

3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official

Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”.

“We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said.

2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official

Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits.

Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later.

He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic.

“If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said.

2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’

Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”.

“The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said.

2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’

Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue.

“Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.”

“There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added.

2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’

The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”.

“Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition.

“It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added.

2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break

1:50pm - Lunch break

The conference will resume at 2:30pm.

1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition.

“As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”.

She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition.

1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty.

“It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said.

1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition

Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition.

She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”.

“Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said.

She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”.

“If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said.

1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important.

She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions.

1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food.

“It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said.

He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said.

12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme

BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry.

He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”.

“This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021.

“Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer.

“So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said.

12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says

Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity.

“We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy.

“Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues.

At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.”

12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins

A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins.

12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia

Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world.

“We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”.

“In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India.

“So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.”

12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth

Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges.

“If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition.

He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity.

“So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention.

“We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said.

12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers

Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme.

“It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership.

“These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.”

11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems

Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region.

“We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said.

He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things.

11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities

The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun.

11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress

Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform.

“It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”.

“We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted.

Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”.

He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition.

“The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official

The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement.

She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”.

Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition.

“This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added.

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.

item.description:
A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations.

View the full agenda here.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.
